It also kills unevenly: people without air conditioning, outdoor workers, and older residents are most at risk.

Buildings designed for a cooler century make the problem worse. Dark roofs absorb sunlight and release heat at night. Wide streets without trees store heat in asphalt. Air conditioning removes heat from inside a building and dumps it outside, which raises the temperature of the street. In dense neighborhoods, the effect can add several degrees. The result is a loop: the hotter it gets, the more energy is used, and the hotter the city becomes.

The simplest solution is also the oldest: trees. A mature tree shades a street and cools the air by releasing water through its leaves. Studies in several cities found that neighborhoods with more canopy can be three to five degrees cooler than neighborhoods without it. Trees also reduce electricity bills and improve air quality. The difficulty is time: a tree takes decades to mature, and the neighborhoods that need shade most often have the fewest trees.

Architecture can help immediately. Light-colored roofs reflect sunlight instead of absorbing it. Insulation keeps heat out during the day and slows its escape at night. Shutters, balconies, and narrow streets, traditional solutions in southern Europe and the Middle East, create shade without using energy. Some new buildings use courtyards and water, although water is scarce in the places that are getting hottest. None of these ideas is new; many were abandoned when air conditioning became cheap.

Some of these measures are being tested at scale. Los Angeles has painted streets with a light coating that reflects sunlight, and early measurements showed a modest drop in surface temperature, although the air above the road changed less than expected. Ahmedabad, in India, wrote a heat action plan after a disaster in 2010, with warnings, water stations, and changes to working hours; researchers estimated that it saved more than a thousand lives a year. Such plans work best when they are simple enough to follow and repeated every summer.

Public space matters as much as private buildings. A city can open cooling centers, keep libraries open late, and provide water in parks. Seville, in Spain, gives its streets names based on ancient winds and has begun to shade public squares with fabric structures. Medellín, in Colombia, built green corridors along roads and rivers, and local temperatures fell. These projects are cheaper than rebuilding a city, and they can be started in a single summer.

The hardest problem is social. Heat deaths are concentrated among people who cannot afford to run an air conditioner or who live in housing without one. Advice to drink water and stay indoors assumes a home that is cool and a job that allows breaks. Some cities now require landlords to provide cooling, and some unions have won the right to stop work in extreme heat. These rules are controversial because they cost money, and because the risk is invisible until someone dies.

There is a limit to adaptation. Beyond a certain combination of heat and humidity, the human body cannot cool itself, even at rest. Researchers call this the wet-bulb limit, and it is being approached in parts of South Asia and the Persian Gulf. In those conditions, air conditioning becomes a matter of survival rather than comfort, which makes electricity a basic service. Adaptation buys time. It does not remove the cause.

The lesson of the last few summers is that heat is a design problem. A city can be built to trap heat or to release it, to expose people or to shade them. The choices are made in budgets, building codes, and tree-planting programs, usually years before anyone notices. Phoenix now has an office of heat response, which sounds strange until you remember that other cities have offices for snow. The climate has changed, and the streets must change with it.

Boredom has a bad reputation. Parents fill children’s days with activities, phones fill every quiet minute, and adults describe an empty afternoon as wasted time. Yet psychologists who study boredom argue that it serves a purpose. It is a signal, like hunger or pain, that something is missing. The discomfort pushes a person to look for stimulation, and sometimes the search produces something new.

The research is more complicated than the popular version. Boredom is not one thing. There is the boredom of a dull task, which can be reduced by changing the task, and there is a deeper boredom in which nothing seems meaningful. The second type is linked to anxiety and depression, and it should not be romanticized. The claim that boredom is good for creativity applies mainly to the first type: a mind that is under-stimulated but not distressed.

Several experiments support the link. In one, participants copied numbers from a phone book, a deliberately boring task. Afterwards they were asked to think of as many uses as possible for a pair of plastic cups. The bored group produced more ideas than a control group that had not done the boring task. The researchers suggested that boredom creates a kind of mental restlessness that seeks an outlet.

Other studies point to a simpler mechanism: time. Creativity needs uninterrupted time, and modern life provides very little of it. A walk without headphones, a train journey without a screen, or a shower produces conditions in which the mind wanders. Mind-wandering is not efficient, but it is how people connect distant ideas. The problem with a phone is not the screen itself; it is that the phone fills every gap where wandering used to happen.

There is a cultural dimension. Some societies treat idleness as a moral failure, while others protect it. The Italian idea of dolce far niente, the sweetness of doing nothing, is not laziness; it is a different attitude to time. In workplaces, visible busyness is often rewarded more than useful thinking, which encourages people to look occupied even when the work is done. Boredom becomes something to hide.

The word itself is relatively new. Historians note that “boredom” appeared in English only in the nineteenth century, along with railways, factories, and the idea of leisure as a problem to be solved. Earlier societies had words for slowness, melancholy, or idleness, but not for the specific discomfort of having nothing to do. Some researchers argue that boredom as we know it is a product of a world that expects constant interest.

The digital environment makes the signal harder to hear. A short video provides stimulation within seconds, so the discomfort never lasts long enough to become a question. Some studies find that people who spend long periods watching short videos report more boredom, not less, as if the habit raises the threshold for interest. That is the paradox: the fastest cure for boredom may make boredom more likely later.

For children, the argument is practical. Play that adults organize is different from play that children invent. When a child complains of boredom, the first response is often a screen, and the screen ends the discomfort immediately. It also ends the search. Teachers report that children who are used to constant stimulation find it harder to stay with a difficult problem, because the first minute of frustration feels unbearable.

None of this means that boredom should be imposed. A person who is bored at work may need a different job, not a philosophy. A teenager who is bored every evening may need friends, exercise, or help. The useful distinction is between boredom that leads somewhere and boredom that traps. The first is a door; the second is a room with no exit, and it deserves attention rather than praise.

The practical suggestion is small. Leave some gaps in the day. Walk without headphones once a week. Put the phone in another room while waiting. These are not moral rules, and they will not make anyone more creative on demand. They simply restore a condition that used to be normal: a mind with nothing to do, for a few minutes, until it finds something on its own. That is not a productivity trick, and it does not need to be.
